rungs.stem: In the Fenian Cycle, the aging warrior-leader Fionn mac Cumhaill -- now older than the High King himself -- is promised in marriage to the young and beautiful daughter of Cormac mac Airt, the High King at Tara. What is the young princess's name?
rungs.context: Grainne (pronounced GRAWN-ya) is the girl who will not have old Fionn. Sadhbh is Fionn's earlier wife, the mother of Oisin (she is a deer under enchantment); Etain is the heroine of Tochmarc Etaine in a different cycle; Emer is Cu Chulainn's wife from the Ulster Cycle. All four are famous women from Irish mythology. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pursuit_of_Diarmuid_and_Grainne.

rungs.stem: One of the finest young warriors in Fionn's own Fianna carries a magical beauty-mark placed on his brow by a faery woman -- the ball seirce, or 'love-spot' -- that makes any woman who catches a glimpse of it fall instantly in love with him. Who is he?
rungs.context: Diarmuid Ua Duibhne (Diarmuid of the love-spot) is one of the finest and most beloved young warriors of the Fianna. Oisin is Fionn's poet son; Caoilte mac Ronain is Fionn's runner-messenger; Goll mac Morna is Fionn's older rival within the Fianna. All four are Fenian heroes, only one carries the ball seirce. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diarmuid_Ua_Duibhne.

rungs.stem: At the betrothal feast at Tara, Grainne looks around the hall at old white-haired Fionn and refuses the match in her heart. She sees Diarmuid across the room -- his love-spot showing under a cap -- and takes decisive action. What does she do to the rest of the hall?
choices: drugs every cup with a sleeping potion
sings a lullaby that puts them to sleep
throws a druidic mist over them
sets a spell of silence on the tables
rungs.answer: drugs every cup with a sleeping potion
rungs.context: Grainne passes the drinking-cups herself, dosing every guest EXCEPT Diarmuid. The sleeping-cup at the feast is one of the most famous images in the tale. The other three -- lullaby-sleep, druidic mist, spell of silence -- are all real motifs elsewhere in Irish myth (druidic mist is very common), but the tool here is a straightforward drugged cup. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pursuit_of_Diarmuid_and_Grainne.

rungs.stem: With the hall asleep, Grainne goes to Diarmuid and speaks. He refuses her at first, out of loyalty to Fionn. So she binds him with an unbreakable magical vow to elope with her that same night, one he cannot refuse. What is the Irish name for this kind of unbreakable vow?
rungs.context: A geis (plural geasa) is an unbreakable magical prohibition or command in Irish myth -- to break it is to invite destruction. Grainne's geis leaves Diarmuid no choice. Fian is the warrior-band itself; rath is a ringfort; ban is a plain English word here (not the Irish word). All four sound Irish and start with the right shape -- only geis is the term for the vow. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pursuit_of_Diarmuid_and_Grainne.

rungs.stem: Bound by the vow, Diarmuid takes Grainne and flees the hall at Tara. Fionn and the Fianna pursue them across Ireland for a very long time -- so long that Ireland's oral tradition remembers the exact count. About how many years does the pursuit last?
rungs.context: The pursuit is remembered as sixteen years -- long enough for Diarmuid and Grainne to have five children on the run. Seven is the standard folk-year (as in the seven years' service of Jacob); three years is the geasa-year; twenty-one is a marker in Fenian tales too. Only sixteen matches Toraigheacht Dhiarmada agus Ghrainne. Source: irishgodsandgoddesses.net/myths/pursuit-of-diarmuid-and-grainne.

rungs.stem: Across Ireland today you can be shown megalithic tombs -- great slab-roofed dolmens -- that country folk have named for the fugitive lovers, saying they slept beneath them during the flight. What is the folk-name given to these dolmens?
choices: the Beds of Diarmuid and Grainne
rungs.answer: the Beds of Diarmuid and Grainne
rungs.context: Leaba Dhiarmada agus Ghrainne ('the Beds of Diarmuid and Grainne') is the folk-name given to dozens of Neolithic dolmens across Ireland. In tradition the couple could never sleep two nights in the same bed -- so they left behind a whole scatter of them. The Cauldron of the Dagda is one of the Four Treasures of the Tuatha; Aengus has famous dwellings but not this name; Fionn has 'seats' and 'tables' in folk-place-lore but not this one. Source: bardmythologies.com/diarmuid-and-grainne.

rungs.stem: Diarmuid's foster-father is one of the Tuatha De Danann -- the god of love, of the Brugh na Boinne on the Boyne. He shelters the fleeing lovers again and again with mist and trickery, and eventually mediates a peace with Fionn. Who is Diarmuid's foster-father?
rungs.context: Aengus Og (Aengus 'the Young') is the god of love, master of the great passage-tomb at Newgrange (Brugh na Boinne). Lugh Lamhfhada is the many-skilled hero; the Dagda is the 'good god' with the club and the cauldron; Manannan mac Lir is the sea-god. All four are Tuatha De Danann -- only Aengus is Diarmuid's foster-father. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diarmuid_Ua_Duibhne.

rungs.stem: Years after the peace, Fionn organises a great boar-hunt on a real Irish mountain in County Sligo -- a limestone table-mountain with a sudden northern cliff, still visible from Sligo town today. It is here that Diarmuid meets his death. Which mountain is it?
rungs.context: Ben Bulben (Beann Ghulbain, 'peak of Gulba') is a real 526-metre limestone mountain in County Sligo, its flat top and prow-like north face famous in Irish landscape (Yeats is buried in its shadow at Drumcliffe). Slieve Bloom is the mountain-range of central Ireland; Cnoc Aine is the fairy-hill of the goddess Aine in Limerick; Slieve Mish is a range in Kerry. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diarmuid_Ua_Duibhne.

rungs.stem: The boar on Ben Bulben is no ordinary beast. It was once a human boy, changed into an enchanted boar by a druid after being killed as a child, and set under a prophecy binding it to be the death of one Fenian warrior. In the boy's identity lies the whole tragedy. WHO was the boy?
choices: a half-brother of the doomed man
a stable-boy of Cormac mac Airt
rungs.answer: a half-brother of the doomed man
rungs.context: The half-brother -- Roc's son -- was killed as a child by Diarmuid's father Donn (crushed between his knees when Donn feared the boy was not his own); the boy's father, the druid Roc, then turned the body into a boar bound by prophecy to be Diarmuid's death. So Fionn's boar-hunt on Ben Bulben deliberately sends Diarmuid against a beast fated by druidic craft to kill him. Source: irishgodsandgoddesses.net/myths/death-of-diarmuid.

rungs.stem: The boar gores Diarmuid, but he mortally wounds it in return. Fionn arrives to find him dying. Long ago Fionn had gained a certain gift from the Salmon of Knowledge -- the ability to heal any wound with something carried a certain way from a nearby well. What can he carry, and how?
choices: a live coal on his tongue
wet moss twisted round his thumb
rungs.context: The healing-water in Fionn's cupped hands is the whole hinge of the death-scene: he CAN save Diarmuid, and the whole Fianna is watching. Salmon-scales, a live coal, and wet moss are all plausible-sounding folk-cures from the wider Irish tradition, but they are not the gift attached to Fionn. Source: irishgodsandgoddesses.net/myths/death-of-diarmuid.

rungs.stem: Fionn walks to the well twice. Both times he brings the healing water back close to Diarmuid, and both times it is gone before it can touch the wound. He goes back a third time and does deliver it -- but by then it is too late. HOW, exactly, does the water get away from Fionn on the first two trips?
choices: it slips through his cupped fingers
it evaporates in the noon sun
his hound-pups drink it from the bowl
a raven of the Morrigan strikes it out of his hand
rungs.answer: it slips through his cupped fingers
rungs.context: Fionn LETS the water fall through his cupped fingers twice on purpose -- remembering Grainne, remembering the sixteen years of pursuit, remembering the humiliation. On the third trip he brings the water, but Diarmuid has already died. It is one of the darkest moments in the Fenian Cycle: the leader murdering a friend by deliberate omission, in front of witnesses. Grainne curses Fionn when she hears, and the Fianna is never the same again. Source: irishgodsandgoddesses.net/myths/death-of-diarmuid.

rungs.stem: The shape of the tale -- an old king, a young queen, a young knight bound by involuntary love to elope with her, and a long pursuit -- is so close to a great Continental romance that scholars regard the Irish tale as its direct ancestor, and debate the direction of borrowing. Which later romance grew from this shape?
rungs.context: Tristan (nephew of old King Mark of Cornwall), the young Irish princess Iseult he escorts home to marry his uncle, the love-potion, the flight into the forest, the pursuit -- the beat-list matches Toraigheacht Dhiarmada agus Ghrainne almost exactly. Most scholars now think the Irish material fed the Continental Tristan through Brittany. Lancelot and Guinevere is a different Arthurian love-triangle; Roland and Aude are the doomed betrothed of the Chanson de Roland; Aucassin and Nicolette is a 13th-c. French chantefable. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pursuit_of_Diarmuid_and_Grainne.
